messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Electrician
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Hopelessness: I have no future, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Darryl, a 42-year-old electrician of Pacific Islander background, had been working long days for years and was used to finishing jobs after dark, when tools were packed away and the streets were quieter. The assault happened on one such evening, at roughly the same time of day he now found hardest to tolerate. He had been leaving a site after a routine call-out when the ordinary sounds around him changed shape in his mind: a door opening somewhere nearby, then slamming sharply, and then the sudden sense that something was wrong. What followed was not recalled by Darryl as a smooth sequence but as a few hard-edged pictures that seemed to sit apart from one another. He described seeing the scene in brief snapshots, each moment like a separate photograph: the place, the threat, his own body in it. Even now, when he tries to think about it, the account never fills in properly. Large parts feel missing, as though he can only reach fragments and the rest has been cut away. What he does remember arrives with an overwhelming sense of guilt. He returns to those moments and feels intensely responsible, as if the assault says something true about the sort of person he is. He was certain, in the aftermath, that somebody else would not have ended up in that situation, and that thought has stayed with him.

In the weeks that followed, Darryl began to notice that the same time of day would bring on a particular shift in how he felt. As evening approached, he would find himself beginning to detach, as if the world had moved a little farther away and he were becoming unreal in it. He did not experience this as an abstract fear but as a bodily, unsettling drift that made him pause and check himself. The change was especially sharp when a door banged somewhere in the house, or when a door at work or in a shop opened too suddenly; the sound would jolt him back into the assault before he could settle. He also became wary of unexpected movement nearby. If someone moved quickly beside him, even in an ordinary setting, his body reacted before he had time to think, as though danger were present again. He found the same thing happening when someone touched him without warning. A hand on his arm, a tap on the shoulder, even a casual brush in passing could bring an immediate alarmed reaction that embarrassed him afterward, though at the moment it felt automatic and unavoidable.

Darryl’s days gradually narrowed around what felt manageable. He began spending long hours on his phone, games, and the internet, letting himself disappear into screens for stretches that were much longer than he intended. At night, and sometimes during breaks, he would keep scrolling or gaming simply so he would not have to think. He also started drinking more than he had before and used medication or drugs at times to blunt what was coming up in his mind. He avoided television programmes, films, and anything he might read that reminded him of similar events, not because he wanted to be uninformed but because he could not bear the images they might bring into his head. In the months after the assault, this pattern affected both his relationship and his work. His partner noticed how often he was off on his phone and how present he was not during conversations, while at work he became more guarded in unfamiliar places. He avoided going to new sites or places he could not assess in advance, feeling he could not judge where the danger might be. That meant he sometimes turned down opportunities or relied on the most familiar routes and settings, limiting the way he moved through both job and daily life.

By the time Darryl came to treatment, he was living with the constant sense that he had no future and that the attack had revealed something final about him. He was not speaking as someone looking back on one bad event but as someone who felt that the event had narrowed his life to a set of predictable alarms, gaps in memory, and a future that had already been taken away. What brought him in was the accumulation of those fears: the startle at doors and movement, the unease when touched, the pull to disappear into screens or drink, and the growing sense that his world was shrinking around what he could no longer face. He came hoping, if possible, to feel less on edge and less trapped by the memory fragments that still arrived at the same hour each day, but he was most afraid that nothing would change and that the assault had already decided who he was and what would happen next.
